title: QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs
finding: Backprop through a frozen 4-bit model into LoRA adapters lets a 65B model be fine-tuned on a single 48GB GPU while preserving full 16-bit fine-tuning task performance (per authors).
why_for_us: Baseline recipe for fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Coder-14B (and fitting larger) on one 32GB RTX 5090; compare against bf16 LoRA on the same data.

title: LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less
finding: On programming and math, standard low-rank LoRA substantially underperforms full fine-tuning (both ~100K instruction pairs and 20B-token continued pretraining), but forgets less outside the target domain; full fine-tuning learns perturbations with 10-100x higher rank than typical LoRA (per authors).
why_for_us: Expect LoRA on a 5090 to give modest in-domain gains; use high rank and measure both our hidden-test acceptance and general-coding regression before trusting a LoRA adapter.

title: DoRA: Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation
finding: Decomposes weights into magnitude and direction to narrow the accuracy gap between LoRA-style PEFT and full fine-tuning without extra inference cost (per authors; no numbers in OpenAlex abstract excerpt).
why_for_us: Drop-in flag in PEFT; cheap A/B against plain LoRA on the same task-card dataset.

title: GaLore: Memory-Efficient LLM Training by Gradient Low-Rank Projection
finding: Projects gradients (not weights) into a low-rank subspace to cut optimizer-state memory while allowing full-parameter learning, addressing LoRA's underperformance vs full-rank training (per authors).
why_for_us: Option for near-full fine-tuning of 7-8B models within 32GB if LoRA plateaus (see L002).

title: Let the Expert Stick to His Last: Expert-Specialized Fine-Tuning for Sparse Architectural Large Language Models
finding: Routing for a given task is highly concentrated on few experts; tuning only the most relevant experts (ESFT) matches or surpasses full-parameter fine-tuning, and finer-grained MoEs benefit more (per authors).
why_for_us: For Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-style MoE: log expert activations on our task cards, then fine-tune only top experts to fit in 32GB.

title: LoRA Soups: Merging LoRAs for Practical Skill Composition Tasks
finding: Studies merging separately trained LoRA modules to compose skills for a target task lacking direct training data (per authors; numbers not in excerpt).
why_for_us: Train small per-skill LoRAs (e.g. Python tests, TS edits) and merge instead of one big run; cheap to try.

title: Does Reinforcement Learning Really Incentivize Reasoning Capacity in LLMs Beyond the Base Model?
finding: RLVR-trained models beat their base at small k (pass@1) but base models reach higher pass@k at large k across math, coding and visual tasks; six popular RLVR algorithms perform similarly, while distillation from a teacher can add genuinely new reasoning patterns (per authors).
why_for_us: Before spending GPU-hours on GRPO, measure base-model pass@k on our task cards; if pass@16 is high, best-of-n with tests or distillation from Claude may beat RL.

title: Spurious Rewards: Rethinking Training Signals in RLVR
finding: GRPO with random rewards raised Qwen2.5-Math-7B on MATH-500 by 21.4 pp vs 29.1 pp with true rewards, via a clipping bias that amplifies pretraining behaviours; such gains often fail on Llama3 or OLMo2 (per authors).
why_for_us: We use Qwen: any RL gain we see must be checked against a random-reward control and on a second model family before we believe it.

title: An Imperfect Verifier is Good Enough: Learning with Noisy Rewards
finding: In multi-seed Qwen3-8B RLVR on MBPP, validation reward stayed within ~1 pp of the clean baseline at up to 20% reward noise and within ~2 pp at 30%; authors caution this is not a general threshold (per authors).
why_for_us: Our flaky or partial test suites can still serve as RL rewards; we need not build perfect verifiers first.

title: Improving Small Language Models for Code Generation with Reinforcement Learning from Verification Feedback
finding: LoRA-based GRPO/GSPO on Qwen3-0.6B and Llama3.2-1B improved MBPP pass@1 by up to 13 pp with a combined unit-test plus Ruff reward; lint-only reward pushed the policy to shorter outputs without better correctness (per authors).
why_for_us: A tiny-budget RLVR pilot fits a 5090; use test+lint reward and track length and error types, not only pass@1.

title: Co-Evolving LLM Coder and Unit Tester via Reinforcement Learning (CURE)
finding: Co-training code and unit-test generation from interaction outcomes without ground-truth code; ReasonFlux-Coder 7B/14B improve code accuracy by 5.3% and Best-of-N accuracy by 9.0% (per authors).
why_for_us: The 14B model is in our size range; a self-test generator would strengthen best-of-n selection on task cards lacking tests.

title: G2RPO-A: Guided Group Relative Policy Optimization with Adaptive Guidance
finding: Notes RLVR gives only modest gains for small models lacking world knowledge, and injects ground-truth reasoning steps into rollouts (adaptive guidance) to compensate (per authors).
why_for_us: If plain GRPO stalls on 7-14B, inject Claude-written partial solutions into rollouts as guidance.

title: Beyond Binary: Turning Partial Success into Dense Verifiable Rewards for Reinforcement Learning in Code Generation
finding: Uses test-case-level partial passes as intrinsic dense verifiable reward instead of sparse suite-level pass/fail or a learned reward model (per authors).
why_for_us: Our test runner already reports per-test results; feed fraction-passed as reward.

title: Scaling Test-Time Compute Without Verification or RL is Suboptimal
finding: Proves that fine-tuning with verifier-based signals (0/1 rewards, verifiers, RL, search) scales better than distilling successful search or thinking traces alone (per authors).
why_for_us: Argues for keeping hidden tests in the loop (rejection sampling, RL) rather than pure SFT on Claude traces.

title: DRIVE: Data Curation Best Practices for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Reward in Competitive Code Generation
finding: Argues RL prompt-set construction matters as much as the algorithm for code RLVR and gives a curation pipeline (per authors; numbers not in excerpt).
why_for_us: Checklist for building our RL prompt set from past task cards (difficulty filtering).

title: OPEN-SWE-TRACES: Advancing Dual-Mode Multilingual Distillation for Software Engineering Agents
finding: 207,489 permissively licensed agent trajectories from 20,000 PRs (OpenHands, SWE-agent); fine-tuned Qwen3-30B-A3B reaches 61.7% SWE-bench Verified, 57.1% Multilingual, 36.8% Pro (per authors).
why_for_us: Ready-made SFT data and a result for exactly our MoE class; candidate base model or data for a LoRA run before collecting our own Claude traces.

title: Yet Even Less Is Even Better For Agentic, Reasoning, and Coding LLMs (STITCH)
finding: Filtering trajectories to decision-critical tokens: up to 63.16% relative improvement on SWE-bench Verified over base models (30B-355B, incl. mini-SWE-agent); with <1K trajectories ArkTS compile pass rose to 61.31% (+43.34%) (per authors).
why_for_us: Suggests a few hundred well-filtered Claude trajectories from our own harness may be enough for a useful LoRA.

title: Thinking Longer, Not Larger: Enhancing Software Engineering Agents via Scaling Test-Time Compute
finding: A 32B model on a single GPU, trained on rejection-sampled synthesized trajectories plus reward-model and execution-guided search at development decision points, reaches 46% on SWE-bench Verified, above DeepSeek R1 671B and o1 (per authors).
why_for_us: Closest published analogue to our setup; replicate their rejection-sampling + execution-verified search on 14-32B.

title: From Patches to Trajectories: Privileged Process Supervision for Software-Engineering Agents
finding: SFT on long teacher trajectories makes the student inherit ungrounded leaps and redundant loops; proposes training data where each step is grounded and efficient (per authors; numbers not in excerpt).
why_for_us: Strip loops and redundant reads from Claude trajectories before SFT.

title: MetaCurate: Evolving Curation Filters for High-Quality Agentic Coding Data
finding: Resolved patches can follow inefficient reasoning and failed runs can hold useful steps, so success-only filtering is insufficient; proposes automatically evolved curation filters (per authors).
why_for_us: Do not keep only accepted runs; score steps and keep useful segments of failed runs too.

title: A Systematic Evaluation of Trajectory Data Curation for LoRA Fine-Tuning of Code Agents
finding: No abstract in the OpenAlex record; keywords indicate a study of quantity-quality trade-offs and dataset-size effects for LoRA SFT of code agents.
why_for_us: Directly matches our plan (LoRA on agent traces); read the PDF before choosing dataset size.

title: Beyond Model Collapse: Scaling Up with Synthesized Data Requires Verification
finding: Verifiers, even imperfect ones, can select synthesized data that prevents model collapse; a proposed proxy measure correlates strongly with downstream performance (per authors).
why_for_us: Our hidden tests plus review are the verifier; never recycle unverified model outputs into training.

title: Is Model Collapse Inevitable? Breaking the Curse of Recursion by Accumulating Real and Synthetic Data
finding: Prior collapse results assumed new synthetic data replaces old data; accumulating real and synthetic data instead avoids collapse (per authors, from title and abstract).
why_for_us: When iterating SFT rounds, keep accumulating human/Claude data rather than replacing with self-generated data.

title: Give Me BF16 or Give Me Death? Accuracy-Performance Trade-Offs in LLM Quantization
finding: Across 500,000+ evaluations on Llama-3.1: FP8 (W8A8) is effectively lossless, tuned INT8 loses 1-3%, INT4 weight-only rivals 8-bit; in vLLM W4A16 is most cost-efficient for synchronous use and W8A8 for continuous batching (per authors).
why_for_us: Single-agent sequential calls on a 5090 favour W4A16 (AWQ/GPTQ); switch to FP8 if we run several agents in parallel.

title: Evaluating the Impact of Post-Training Quantization on Large Language Models for Code Generation
finding: For code LLMs up to 34B, 4-bit quantization cuts memory ~70% on average with no significant loss; at 3 and 2 bits a code-specific calibration set limits the loss (per authors).
why_for_us: 4-bit 32-35B models on 32GB are a sound default; if we ever go below 4-bit, calibrate on our own repos.

title: Is Quantization a Deal-Breaker? Empirical Insights From Large Code Models
finding: AWQ-quantized CodeLlama and DeepSeekCoder pass tests at rates comparable to unquantized models and preserve maintainability and complexity metrics in Java and Python (per authors).
why_for_us: Supports AWQ for our cheap worker; add a static-analysis check to review to catch quality drift.

title: EAGLE-3: Scaling up Inference Acceleration of Large Language Models via Training-Time Test
finding: Direct token prediction with multi-layer feature fusion gives speedups up to 6.5x, about 1.4x over EAGLE-2, and 1.38x throughput at batch 64 in SGLang (per authors).
why_for_us: If an EAGLE-3 draft head exists for our Qwen model, enable it in vLLM/SGLang and measure tokens/s and $/accepted change.

title: SpecForge: A Flexible and Efficient Open-Source Training Framework for Speculative Decoding
finding: Open-source, production-oriented framework for training EAGLE-3 draft models, addressing the lack of draft models and training infrastructure (per authors).
why_for_us: Route to train our own draft head if none is published for the exact Qwen checkpoint we serve.

title: REST: Retrieval-Based Speculative Decoding
finding: No abstract text in the OpenAlex record; keywords indicate speculative decoding with drafts retrieved from a datastore instead of a draft model.
why_for_us: Code edits reuse existing file text; retrieval/n-gram drafting needs no extra VRAM; test via vLLM n-gram speculation.

title: The N-Grammys: Accelerating Autoregressive Inference with Learning-Free Batched Speculation
finding: Learning-free, negligible-cost drafts from n-grams (from weights and context): the true next token is rarely the top n-gram prediction but often within its top-k for small k (per authors).
why_for_us: Zero-training speedup candidate for edit-heavy agent turns; benchmark prompt-lookup vs no speculation on our traces.

title: KVQuant: Towards 10 Million Context Length LLM Inference with KV Cache Quantization
finding: KV cache dominates memory at long context; KVQuant enables accurate sub-4-bit KV quantization where previous methods failed (per authors).
why_for_us: Long agent contexts on 32GB: test FP8 KV cache in vLLM and check acceptance rate does not drop.

title: Break Later or Never: Prefix-Preserving Context Compaction for Coding Agents
finding: Uncompacted agent trajectories get 98-99% prefix-cache reuse; masking old observations in batches every few steps keeps 95-98% reuse while cutting context up to 50%, serving cost up to 18% and completion time up to 21%; KV-level ObsDrop reaches 2.45-2.85x throughput (per authors).
why_for_us: Our compaction must not rewrite the prefix each turn; implement batched masking in the harness and measure vLLM prefix-cache hit rate.

title: XGrammar: Flexible and Efficient Structured Generation Engine for Large Language Models
finding: Context-free-grammar constrained decoding is expensive because of per-token stack-state checks over the vocabulary; XGrammar is an engine that makes it efficient (per authors).
why_for_us: Constrain tool-call JSON from the cheap model to cut malformed-call retries; check overhead in vLLM.

title: JSONSchemaBench: A Rigorous Benchmark of Structured Outputs for Language Models
finding: Systematic evaluation of constrained-decoding frameworks on JSON Schema, noting little prior evaluation of their behaviour and performance (per authors).
why_for_us: Reference to pick a structured-output backend before enforcing tool schemas.

title: FrugalGPT: How to Use Large Language Models While Reducing Cost and Improving Performance
finding: LLM API prices differ by two orders of magnitude; proposes cascade-type strategies to cut cost while maintaining or improving quality (per authors).
why_for_us: Foundational framing for our cheap-first, Claude-escalate design.

title: RouteLLM: Learning to Route LLMs with Preference Data
finding: Routers trained on preference data cut cost by over 2x in some cases without compromising quality, and transfer when the strong/weak models change (per authors).
why_for_us: Train a small router on our logged accept/reject outcomes to decide which task cards go to the 5090 model vs Claude.

title: A Unified Approach to Routing and Cascading for LLMs
finding: Unifies routing (one model per query) and cascading (sequentially larger models) with formal optimality analysis (per authors).
why_for_us: Theory for combining up-front routing with escalate-on-failure.

title: CodeRescue: Budget-Calibrated Recovery Routing for Coding Agents
finding: After a failed attempt, cheap-model retry and escalation succeed on complementary cases; a router with conformal risk control beats fixed policies, and one calibrated point exceeds always-escalate solve rate at 35% of its mean recovery cost (GPT-5.4-nano/GPT-5.4) (per authors).
why_for_us: On test failure, decide 'retry cheap with feedback' vs 'escalate to Claude' with a learned rule instead of a fixed retry count.

title: The Handoff Tax: Continuing Non-Native Trajectories in LLM Agents
finding: With Claude and GPT cheap/strong pairs, escalating mid-run with the full trajectory recovers less than half of the quality gap at a substantial cost premium; downshifting is favourable; giving the strong model less of the cheap model's trajectory improves escalation (per authors).
why_for_us: When escalating a failed card to Claude, pass repo state plus a short summary, not the cheap model's full transcript; prefer Claude-plans then cheap-executes.

title: Scrouting: Cost-Aware Routing of Coding Agents by Scouting the Repository First
finding: A 7B searcher explores the repo first and produces a sandbox-verified handoff; its hidden states plus task text drive routing, instead of routing from issue text alone (per authors).
why_for_us: Let the cheap model scout and reproduce first, then route by what it found.

title: BEST-Route: Adaptive LLM Routing with Test-Time Optimal Compute
finding: Routes to a model and also chooses how many samples to draw from a small model, since a single small-model response often loses to the large model (per authors).
why_for_us: Joint choice: N samples from the cheap model vs one Claude call per task card.

title: The Complexity Trap: Simple Observation Masking Is as Efficient as LLM Summarization for Agent Context Management
finding: In SWE-agent on SWE-bench Verified over five model configs, masking old observations halves cost vs the raw agent while matching LLM summarization solve rate; a hybrid cuts a further 7% vs masking and 11% vs summarization (per authors).
why_for_us: Implement observation masking in our mini-SWE-agent harness before any LLM summarizer.

title: Reducing Cost of LLM Agents with Trajectory Reduction (AgentDiet)
finding: Removing useless, redundant and expired trajectory content cuts input tokens 39.9-59.7% and total cost 21.1-35.9% with unchanged agent performance (two LLMs, two benchmarks) (per authors).
why_for_us: Prune stale file views and repeated test logs; directly lowers both Claude and 5090 token costs.

title: ACON: Optimizing Context Compression for Long-horizon LLM Agents
finding: Unbounded context growth causes memory cost and reasoning degradation; ACON optimizes compression guidelines rather than relying on brittle heuristics (per authors).
why_for_us: Later step if simple masking (L042) is not enough for long cards.

title: Analyzing and Mitigating Cost-Inefficient Behaviors in Coding Agents
finding: Across Claude Code and Mini-SWE-Agent trajectories, subsumed retrieval, similar-script generation and test re-execution affect 79-98% of tasks and up to 22.75% of cost; structure-aware retrieval can raise cost up to 28.14%; developer-designed skills cut cost up to 41.73% (per authors).
why_for_us: Write hand-made skills/guidance for our harness; be wary of adding code-graph retrieval tools without measuring cost.

title: EET: Experience-Driven Early Termination for Cost-Efficient Software Engineering Agents
finding: Experience-guided early termination cuts total cost 19-55% (32% average) on SWE-bench Verified across three agents with at most 0.2% loss in resolution rate (per authors).
why_for_us: Stop hopeless cheap-model runs early using signals from our past runs; saves GPU minutes per accepted change.

title: More with Less: An Empirical Study of Turn-Control Strategies for Efficient Coding Agents
finding: Studies turn limits and related strategies, noting cost grows quadratically with turns and agents take unnecessary steps (per authors; numbers not in excerpt).
why_for_us: Tune max-turns per task-card type instead of one global cap.

title: One Tool Is Enough: Reinforcement Learning for Repository-Level LLM Agents (RepoNavigator)
finding: A single execution-aware tool, jump-to-definition of an invoked symbol, replaces multiple auxiliary retrieval tools for repository localization (per authors; numbers not in excerpt).
why_for_us: Add one go-to-definition tool (e.g. via tree-sitter or LSP) to the cheap agent's ACI instead of a full code graph.

title: LocAgent: Graph-Guided LLM Agents for Code Localization
finding: Represents codebases as graphs for multi-hop localization from natural-language issues (per authors; numbers not in OpenAlex abstract).
why_for_us: Reference point for graph-based vs grep localization; compare against L045's warning on retrieval overhead.

title: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?
finding: No abstract in the OpenAlex record; keywords indicate a study and taxonomy of failure modes of multi-agent LLM systems.
why_for_us: Use the failure taxonomy to label our planner-worker-reviewer handoff failures.

title: Capable language models can outgrow the benefits of collaboration
finding: Across 260 configurations with fixed prompts, tools and compute, single-agent baseline performance best predicts whether coordination helps; a capability-saturation threshold predicted the effect in 94% of validation configs on SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench, and the model picks the best architecture in 87% of held-out configs (per authors).
why_for_us: Multi-agent structure helps weak agents more; measure single-agent acceptance first and drop extra roles where it is already high.

title: Single-Agent LLMs Outperform Multi-Agent Systems on Multi-Hop Reasoning Under Equal Thinking Token Budgets
finding: With reasoning tokens held constant, single agents match or beat multi-agent systems on multi-hop reasoning (Qwen3, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama, Gemini 2.5); many reported MAS gains come from unaccounted compute and API budget artifacts (per authors).
why_for_us: Any multi-agent variant we test must be compared at equal token/GPU budget.

title: Scaling Test-time Compute for LLM Agents
finding: Test-time scaling improves agents; knowing when to reflect matters; list-wise verification/merging performs best; more diverse rollouts help (per authors).
why_for_us: For best-of-n on task cards, use list-wise selection over candidates and diversify rollouts (temperature, prompts).

title: Can 1B LLM Surpass 405B LLM? Rethinking Compute-Optimal Test-Time Scaling
finding: Compute-optimal test-time scaling depends on policy, PRM and difficulty; with it a 1B model exceeds a 405B model on MATH-500, a 3B beats 405B and a 7B beats o1 and DeepSeek-R1 on MATH-500 and AIME24 (per authors).
why_for_us: Math-only, but supports spending 5090 time on sampling plus test-verification instead of buying a bigger model; tune n per difficulty.

title: Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: Studies how much a fixed inference-time compute budget can improve LLM outputs, comparing it with scaling parameters (per authors; numbers not in excerpt).
why_for_us: Foundational reference for allocating samples adaptively per task difficulty.

title: Adding Error Bars to Evals: A Statistical Approach to Language Model Evaluations
finding: Treats eval questions as drawn from a super-population and gives formulas for analysing and planning evaluations as experiments (per authors).
why_for_us: Report acceptance rate with CIs and use paired comparisons on the same task cards for every harness change.

title: Position: Don't Use the CLT in LLM Evals With Fewer Than a Few Hundred Datapoints
finding: On small specialised benchmarks, CLT-based error bars dramatically underestimate uncertainty; recommends simple frequentist and Bayesian alternatives with a Python library (per authors).
why_for_us: Our eval sets are tens of cards; use Bayesian/exact intervals, not mean +/- 1.96 SE.

title: Measuring all the noises of LLM Evals
finding: Separates prediction noise (resampling answers) from data noise (question sampling); paired prediction noise typically exceeds data noise, so averaging several runs per question substantially raises statistical power (per authors).
why_for_us: Run each task card 3-5 times per configuration and compare paired; cheaper than adding new cards.

title: How to Correctly Report LLM-as-a-Judge Evaluations
finding: Imperfect judge sensitivity and specificity bias naive scores; a plug-in correction with a human-labelled calibration set gives confidence intervals covering both sources of uncertainty (per authors).
why_for_us: If Claude review is used as a metric, hand-label ~50 reviews to calibrate and correct its accept rate.

title: CodeJudgeBench: Benchmarking LLM-as-a-Judge for Coding Tasks
finding: Across 26 judges, small reasoning models (e.g. Qwen3-8B) can beat non-reasoning models up to 70B, but all judges are unstable to response ordering, variable naming and misleading comments (per authors).
why_for_us: A local Qwen3-8B judge is a cheap pre-filter, but randomise candidate order and never rely on judge alone without hidden tests.

title: Justice or Prejudice? Quantifying Biases in LLM-as-a-Judge
finding: Identifies 12 potential biases in LLM-as-a-Judge and an automated quantification framework (CALM) (per authors).
why_for_us: Checklist of judge biases to probe in our Claude reviewer prompts.

title: LiveCodeBench: Holistic and Contamination Free Evaluation of Large Language Models for Code
finding: Continuously collects new problems over time so models can be evaluated on problems released after their training cutoff (per authors).
why_for_us: Pattern for our own eval: keep task cards from our repos dated after the model's release, refreshed monthly.

title: LessLeak-Bench: A First Investigation of Data Leakage in LLMs Across 83 Software Engineering Benchmarks
finding: Investigates leakage of evaluation data into LLM pretraining across 83 SE benchmarks (per authors; numbers not in excerpt).
why_for_us: Reason to trust our private hidden tests over public benchmark scores when choosing the worker model.

title: Lessons from the Trenches on Reproducible Evaluation of Language Models
finding: Three years of evaluation experience: sensitivity to setup, hard cross-method comparisons and lack of reproducibility, with recommended practices (per authors).
why_for_us: Pin prompts, sampling params, backend version and seeds in every experiment log.

title: The Tokenizer Tax Across 25 European Languages
finding: Tokens per word range from 1.2 for English to about 3.1 for Greek/Maltese; Slavic languages sit at 2.2-2.5, and rankings are domain-invariant (rho > 0.97) across ten tokenizers (per authors).
why_for_us: Polish task descriptions and docs cost roughly 2x English tokens; write task cards and agent prompts in English, keep Polish only in user-facing strings.

title: Do All Languages Cost the Same? Tokenization in the Era of Commercial Language Models
finding: Per-token API pricing combined with large cross-language variance in tokens needed for the same content makes some languages costlier (per authors).
why_for_us: Foundational reference for the Polish token premium in our Claude bills.

title: Bielik v3 Small: Technical Report
finding: 1.5B and 4.5B Polish models with a custom Polish tokenizer (APT4) improving token efficiency, trained on 292B tokens; the 4.5B is competitive with models 2-3x its size (per authors).
why_for_us: Cheap local model for Polish-language sub-tasks (legal text extraction, UI copy) that fits beside a coder model on one GPU.

title: Advancing Polish Language Modeling through Tokenizer Optimization in the Bielik v3 7B and 11B Series
finding: Argues universal multilingual tokenizers are architecturally inefficient for Polish and replaces them in Bielik v3 7B/11B (per authors; numbers not in excerpt).
why_for_us: If we serve Polish text at volume, a Polish-tokenizer model cuts tokens and latency per document.

title: Bielik-Q2-Sharp: A Comparative Study of Extreme 2-bit Quantization Methods for a Polish 11B Language Model
finding: Best 2-bit variant (QuIP#) scored 71.92% across 22 Polish benchmarks vs 72.07% for IQ2_XXS; rotation-based methods preserved log-likelihood quality but failed catastrophically at generation; done by one researcher on rented GPUs for $285 (per authors).
why_for_us: Shows a rented-GPU budget study is feasible, and warns to evaluate quantized models on generation, not only multiple-choice log-likelihood.

title: PLLuM: A Family of Polish Large Language Models
finding: Open Polish model family built on a new 140B-token corpus, 77k instructions and 100k preference pairs, with a Responsible AI and data-governance framework and a public-administration use case (per authors).
why_for_us: Alternative Polish model with documented data governance, relevant where GDPR/provenance matters.

title: LLMzSzŁ: a comprehensive LLM benchmark for Polish
finding: Nearly 19k closed-ended questions from Polish national exams across 4 exam types and 154 domains (per authors).
why_for_us: Quick Polish-competence check when choosing or quantizing a Polish-capable model.
